questions.q: What is the normal serum creatinine range?
questions.explain: It rises when GFR falls, but only after about half of nephron function is lost.

open.q: What is the normal serum creatinine range?

questions.q: What is the normal inulin clearance?

open.q: What is the normal inulin clearance?

questions.explain: About 625 ml/min in a normal adult.

questions.q: What does a fixed urine specific gravity of about 1.010 indicate?
options: Loss of concentrating and diluting ability (isosthenuria)
questions.explain: The urine has the same osmolality as plasma. It is typical of advanced chronic kidney disease.

open.q: What does a fixed urine specific gravity of about 1.010 indicate?

questions.q: What is the normal range of urine specific gravity?
questions.explain: It rises with dehydration and falls in water diuresis.

open.q: What is the normal range of urine specific gravity?

questions.q: What is the normal adult urine output?
questions.explain: It depends on fluid intake and losses.

open.q: What is the normal adult urine output?

questions.explain: Below about 400 ml/day, the kidney cannot excrete the daily solute load.

questions.q: Give an example of a cause of prerenal acute kidney injury.
questions.explain: Prerenal failure follows reduced renal perfusion, before the kidney itself is damaged.

open.q: Give an example of a cause of prerenal acute kidney injury.
open.a: Haemorrhage, dehydration or shock (reduced renal perfusion)

questions.q: Give an example of a cause of postrenal acute kidney injury.
options: Urinary tract obstruction, such as prostate enlargement or stones
questions.explain: Obstruction below the kidneys raises pressure in Bowman's capsule and stops filtration.

open.q: Give an example of a cause of postrenal acute kidney injury.
open.a: Urinary tract obstruction, e.g. enlarged prostate, stones or stricture

questions.q: Name the phases of acute tubular necrosis in order.
questions.explain: Urine falls first, then tubules start to recover and pass large volumes, then function returns.

open.q: Name the phases of acute tubular necrosis in order.

questions.q: Which electrolyte disturbance in renal failure can cause cardiac arrest?
questions.explain: Failure to excrete K⁺ plus acidosis raises plasma K⁺. Tall T waves on ECG are an early sign.

open.q: Which electrolyte disturbance in renal failure can cause cardiac arrest?

questions.q: Why does chronic kidney disease cause anaemia?
questions.explain: Damaged kidneys make too little erythropoietin. Uraemia also shortens red cell lifespan.

open.q: Why does chronic kidney disease cause anaemia?

options: Low calcitriol with hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia
questions.explain: The diseased kidney cannot make calcitriol or excrete phosphate, so secondary hyperparathyroidism develops.

questions.q: What is the term for the syndrome caused by retained nitrogenous waste in kidney failure?
questions.explain: Features include nausea, itching, confusion, pericarditis and bleeding tendency.

open.q: What is the term for the syndrome caused by retained nitrogenous waste in kidney failure?

questions.q: What are the main features of nephrotic syndrome?
questions.explain: Hyperlipidaemia is also typical. The nephritic syndrome has haematuria, hypertension and oliguria instead.

open.q: What are the main features of nephrotic syndrome?

questions.q: Which blood tests are used to assess kidney function?
questions.explain: Urine examination (volume, specific gravity, colour, glucose, microscopy) and clearance tests such as inulin, creatinine and PAH look at function more directly.

open.q: Which blood tests are used to assess kidney function?

questions.q: Which finding on urine microscopy points to kidney (parenchymal) disease?
options: A few squamous cells from the urethra
questions.explain: Casts are moulds of the tubular lumen, so they originate in the kidney.

open.q: Which finding on urine microscopy points to kidney (parenchymal) disease?
